Newborn Care

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: lungs, treatment and follow-up

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a defect in the muscle separating the chest from the abdomen. Abdominal organs can enter the chest before birth and interfere with lung development. It can be life-threatening, but its severity varies. Care involves supporting the lungs and circulation as well as repairing the diaphragm, followed by an individual plan for growth and development.

What changes in the diaphragm and chest

The diaphragm is a broad sheet of muscle and tissue used for breathing. In CDH, part has not formed normally, leaving an opening; occasionally a much larger area is missing. The stomach, intestines, liver or spleen may pass through into the chest. It is a developmental condition, not the same as an abdominal-wall hernia.

The displaced organs reduce the space available for developing lungs. The lung on the affected side is often smaller, but the other lung can also be underdeveloped. CDH is uncommon; estimates are roughly one in 2,500–3,000 births, with variation between populations and how cases are counted.

Pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension

Pulmonary hypoplasia means that the lungs have not developed fully, including their tiny air sacs, called alveoli, and blood vessels. Alveoli are different from bronchi, the larger airways. Smaller lungs have less capacity for gas exchange; this is not simply a problem of air sacs emptying because of missing surfactant.

The lung blood vessels can remain narrow and resistant to blood flow, producing pulmonary hypertension and strain on the heart. This can reduce oxygen delivery even when breathing is supported. Surfactant is not a routine treatment for CDH itself; the neonatal team decides whether a separate indication, such as prematurity-related respiratory distress, exists.

Bochdalek, Morgagni and variable severity

The most common form, Bochdalek hernia, involves the back and side of the diaphragm, usually on the left. Morgagni hernia is towards the front. Right-sided, bilateral and other uncommon defects also occur. The location alone cannot predict how an individual baby will do.

Morgagni hernias are often less symptomatic at birth and can be discovered later, but they are not automatically harmless. Severity depends on lung and blood-vessel development, defect size, the organs involved and any other conditions. Some children have no early symptoms; others need intensive treatment immediately after birth.

Causes, associated conditions and family questions

For many babies, no single cause is identified. Changes in chromosomes or genes can contribute, sometimes as part of a wider syndrome, while other cases appear isolated. Possible genetic and environmental contributions do not mean that something a parent did caused the condition.

A specialist assessment looks for other differences, particularly in the heart, and discusses genetic testing and counselling. Tests and recurrence advice depend on the findings and family history. Neither every Bochdalek hernia nor every CDH diagnosis means that another major condition is inevitable.

Finding CDH before or after birth

Prenatal ultrasound often identifies abdominal organs in the chest. A fetal-medicine team may use detailed ultrasound, fetal echocardiography and sometimes MRI to assess anatomy, lung size and liver position. Genetic testing can be offered after counselling. These findings help plan care but cannot give a certain individual outcome.

After birth, breathing difficulty or abnormal examination findings may lead to a chest X-ray, oxygen and blood-gas assessment and an echocardiogram. Later-presenting children may have breathing, feeding or abdominal symptoms. A normal-looking baby or a previous reassuring scan does not rule out every diaphragmatic defect.

Newborn symptoms and a safe birth plan

Possible signs include fast or difficult breathing, a fast heartbeat, blue or grey colour, an uneven-looking chest and a sunken-looking abdomen. These signs are not specific to CDH. A newborn with breathing difficulty needs immediate medical assessment, not an outpatient wait to see whether the symptoms settle.

When CDH is known before birth, the team plans delivery where specialist neonatal care and paediatric surgery are available, or arranges an appropriate transfer pathway. Discuss who will attend the birth and how you can stay informed. Timing and mode of delivery depend on the pregnancy and local specialist plan; a caesarean is not automatically required solely because of CDH.

Stabilization comes before repair

The neonatal team first supports breathing, oxygenation and circulation. A breathing tube and ventilator may be needed, and a tube into the stomach helps remove swallowed air and fluid. Gentle ventilation and monitoring aim to protect small lungs. Pulmonary-hypertension medicines are selected according to the baby's heart and circulation findings.

Some babies need extracorporeal life support, often called ECMO, temporarily supporting oxygenation and circulation outside the body. It is a specialist option with significant risks, not a cure or a treatment every baby needs. Advice about professional delivery-room equipment is not a reason for a caregiver to withhold emergency first aid.

Surgery and the limited role of fetal intervention

Repair is generally undertaken once the baby is physiologically stable enough. The surgeon returns organs to the abdomen and closes the diaphragm, sometimes using a patch for a larger defect. The approach and timing are individual. Closing the opening does not immediately make underdeveloped lungs normal, so intensive care may continue afterwards.

Selected pregnancies may be assessed at an experienced fetal-treatment centre for temporary fetal tracheal balloon occlusion, called FETO. Trials in isolated left-sided CDH found a survival benefit in selected severe disease, while the moderate-disease trial did not establish a clear benefit. FETO increases membrane-rupture and preterm-birth risks and has balloon-removal risks; it is not routine treatment, a diaphragm repair or a guaranteed outcome.

Breathing, reflux, feeding and growth after hospital care

Some children have ongoing lung disease, need prescribed oxygen or medicines after discharge, or continue treatment for pulmonary hypertension. Follow the written oxygen and medication plan and ask how to respond to changes. Do not reduce support because a child looks comfortable without checking with the team.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux can contribute to vomiting, feeding difficulty and respiratory symptoms. Growth may be affected by higher energy needs and difficulty taking enough milk or food. A dietitian and feeding specialist can help; some children need tube feeding. Reflux treatment and feeding support are tailored, rather than the same medicine or procedure for every child.

Development, hearing and lifelong surveillance

Motor, language or learning difficulties can emerge, and hearing problems may appear later. Developmental assessment, hearing surveillance and early therapies can help address needs. Children follow different paths; reaching every milestone later and then inevitably catching up is not something that can be promised.

Follow-up also checks for hernia recurrence, bowel obstruction and chest or spine problems. The 2026 AAP report recommends risk-based multidisciplinary follow-up, with more intensive care for higher-risk survivors and transition planning into adult care. Surgery does not remove every future risk, and the schedule depends on the child's course and local services.

Choosing care and preparing for home

Care can involve fetal medicine, neonatology, paediatric surgery, cardiology, lung specialists, nutrition, feeding, developmental and genetic services, working with primary care. Ask who coordinates appointments and what local support is available. A hospital's historical case counts or survival comparisons cannot predict your baby's outcome.

Before discharge, ask for written feeding, medicines, oxygen or tube-care instructions, emergency contacts and follow-up dates. Practise any equipment care with the team. Families may also need psychological support, interpretation and practical help with travel or time away from work. Prognosis should be discussed using the baby's actual findings, not a single online percentage.

Changes that should not wait

Seek immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor, floppiness, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness or a seizure. Green vomit, especially after abdominal surgery, also needs immediate emergency assessment; do not wait for a routine CDH appointment. Do not drive yourself to emergency: ask another adult to drive or call an ambulance.

Contact the child's team promptly about worsening feeding, repeated vomiting, poor weight gain or a new change in exercise tolerance, even without emergency signs. Follow any stricter individual discharge instructions. Do not assume a new breathing or abdominal problem is ordinary reflux, or adjust oxygen, medicines or tube feeds on your own.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the fetal or neonatal team to explain the defect, lung and heart findings, any genetic-testing choices and the delivery or transfer plan.

Before going home, practise prescribed feeding or equipment care and obtain written medicine, oxygen, emergency and follow-up instructions.

Keep growth, breathing, feeding, hearing and developmental appointments; seek immediate help for the listed emergencies and ask early about new concerns.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record questions for the care team, feeding or symptom observations and appointment dates. It cannot interpret fetal lung measurements, monitor oxygenation, diagnose recurrence or change treatment. Seek care for warning signs regardless of what an app record shows.

When to seek help

CDH may be life-threatening. Breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor, floppiness, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness, a seizure or green vomit need immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself; ask another adult to drive or call an ambulance. Follow the child's individual plan, contact the team promptly about feeding or growth changes, and do not alter oxygen, medicines or tube feeds without advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • CDH affects diaphragm, lung and pulmonary blood-vessel development; repairing the opening is one part of care.
  • Bochdalek is the common posterior form; Morgagni may present later but still needs specialist assessment.
  • Stabilization usually comes before surgery; ECMO and fetal intervention are options for selected situations.
  • Breathing, reflux, nutrition, growth, hearing and development need an individual follow-up plan.
  • Breathing difficulty, abnormal colour or responsiveness, a seizure or green vomit need immediate emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms can CDH cause?

Newborns may breathe rapidly or with difficulty, have blue or grey colour, a fast heartbeat, an uneven chest or a sunken-looking abdomen. Some defects cause later or no early symptoms. Breathing difficulty needs immediate assessment; symptoms alone cannot identify the cause.

Why does CDH happen?

Often there is no single identified cause. Some cases involve chromosome or gene changes or a wider syndrome. Specialist genetic advice can clarify testing and recurrence for a particular family, without assuming that a parent's actions caused it.

What are the main types?

Bochdalek is at the back and side of the diaphragm and is the commonest form; Morgagni is towards the front. Other locations and bilateral defects occur. A Morgagni diagnosis does not automatically mean that no treatment or follow-up is needed.

What is pulmonary hypoplasia?

It means underdeveloped lungs, including alveoli and blood vessels, and can affect both lungs. Alveoli are air sacs, not bronchi. Pulmonary hypertension adds a circulation problem. Routine surfactant does not correct the whole structural condition.

Does surgery cure the breathing problem straight away?

Surgery closes the diaphragmatic opening after stabilization, sometimes with a patch. The lungs and circulation can still need treatment afterwards. Recovery and long-term needs vary, so repair does not guarantee immediate normal breathing.

Is fetal surgery suitable for every baby?

No. FETO is considered only in selected pregnancies at experienced centres. Severe and moderate trial results differ, and membrane rupture, prematurity and balloon-removal complications matter. Most planning still includes specialist care at birth and postnatal repair.

Will my child catch up in growth and development?

Many children make progress, but no single course is guaranteed. Feeding support, sometimes through a tube, and developmental and hearing follow-up help identify and treat needs early. The team can discuss an individual outlook.

When should we seek urgent help after discharge?

Breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor, floppiness, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness, a seizure or green vomit need immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself; ask another adult to drive or call an ambulance. New feeding or growth concerns need prompt contact with the team, and individual emergency instructions take priority.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
